# @bitakit/packages

An optional host adapter for activating trusted BitaKit packages. Core owns dependencies,
cleanup and readiness. The root entry is headless and browser-safe; optional `/browser` and
`/server` entries provide external artifact delivery and privileged Node installation.
The existing build-catalog API remains unchanged.

## A catalog generated by Discovery

Install the package in the host project first. Its exported `bitakit.plugin` factory and CSS
must follow the normal package contract. Choose packages for lazy activation in the host config:

```ts
// bitakit.config.ts
import { defineBitaKit } from '@bitakit/discovery';

export default defineBitaKit({ catalog: ['notes-plugin'] });
```

Discovery emits `packageCatalog` in `src/bitakit.gen.config.ts` (or `bitakit.gen.ts` in a plain
host). It records the installed version and a literal dynamic import of the public plugin
entry. Catalog packages are omitted from the initial runtime composition. Their type maps and
audited CSS remain included in the build. Packages requiring host configuration remain eager.

```ts
// Host management code, outside plugin hooks, Actions and disposers.
import { createPackageHost } from '@bitakit/packages';
import { packageCatalog } from './bitakit.gen.config';

await runtime.ready;
const packages = createPackageHost({ runtime, catalog: packageCatalog });

const result = await packages.reconcile({
  scope: 'preview-session-1',
  packages: [{ name: 'notes-plugin', version: packageCatalog['notes-plugin'].version }],
});

if (result.status === 'applied') {
  console.log(packages.get()); // Actual owned plugin IDs and Core readiness.
}

// Release the selected packages; unrelated host plugins stay mounted.
await packages.reconcile({ scope: 'preview-session-1', packages: [] });
```

`runtime` is the host's existing mounted runtime. Create one adapter per runtime and manage
its packages through that adapter. Do not simultaneously mutate their definitions through a
second adapter or direct Core calls. Existing host-owned plugins are never adopted implicitly.

A manually composed catalog may return multiple plugin definitions from one loader. They are
added together, so required providers can start before their consumers regardless of array
order. Packages must have disjoint plugin IDs. Shared dependencies belong in the host or in
one separately selected catalog package; overlapping ownership is rejected, not reference-counted.

## Catalog selection and lifetime

`reconcile({ scope, packages })` accepts an **already-authorized active selection**. It does not
save installation records. The host decides which installed records are enabled, authorizes
that choice on the server, and supplies an opaque scope-generation key. A client-provided
scope string is not proof of identity, membership or permission. Persistence scope and the
production authorization service are separate host decisions.

- A changed scope releases all managed plugins before loading the new scope, even when both
  select the same package. Hide the outgoing scope and await the result before revealing the
  new one. A blocked/failed switch still reports the actual previous scope.
- Pending imports are superseded by newer selections. A late result cannot register plugins;
  the newer request need not wait for the old import. Native module evaluation itself cannot
  be cancelled. Module top-levels and catalog factories must be free of external side effects.
- Lifecycle work is awaited and never overlapped. Calls while Core is starting, updating or
  stopping return `blocked`; retry after that operation settles. This also prevents a startup
  hook from queueing management behind itself. Never await management from an affected Action
  or disposer: its cleanup may need that caller to finish.
- Unknown names, versions and duplicate selections are rejected before changing ownership.
  Each catalog name has one build-pinned version. Changing that version requires a new build;
  this adapter does not upgrade packages in place.
- Removal refuses active external dependents. Include dependent managed packages in the
  removal, or explicitly arrange their lifetime first. Core's direct disable/enable API is
  available for host-owned plugins, with its separate retained-settings behavior.

Results are `applied`, `blocked`, `failed`, `restart-required`, or `superseded`, plus `scope`
and `reasons`. Check the result and `get()` after failure. Loading, removal and startup are not
an atomic transaction: removed plugins are not silently restored. A clean failed start retains
truthful ownership and can be retried with the same selection; failed cleanup blocks reuse.

## Catalog boundaries

The catalog is an allowlist of code already trusted by the application operator. It is not a
sandbox. Catalog mode does not download code or upgrade versions. External installation is an explicit
opt-in through the separate entries below; neither mode implements a marketplace or sandbox. Use a separate isolation
boundary for untrusted code.

Unloading releases Core-owned services, Actions, listeners and slot attachments. It cannot
un-evaluate an ES module, evict the browser's import cache, undo external effects, or remove
shared eager styles. Persistent setting records are not deleted. Loader results no longer
owned by the adapter are released; the platform still controls its module cache.

See the [plugin manager guide](../../apps/docs/content/docs/plugin-management.mdx#what-can-change-live) for supported
plugin shapes and restart-required cases. Ordinary provider/config changes still use the
existing host composition replacement mechanism.

## Static identity and provenance

Catalog names compare lowercase with scopes preserved. A catalog entry may declare the complete
`pluginIds` set; known collisions fail before any new load and returned IDs must match. Legacy
loaders without that set retain post-load validation and may still return multiple plugins.
Each loaded definition receives package provenance while retaining a generated loader's membership
and canonical metadata. See the [identity reference](../../apps/docs/content/docs/reference/plugin-metadata.mdx).

## External packages

Install the optional Node toolchain only in the privileged host:

```sh
npm install @bitakit/packages @bitakit/discovery esbuild rollup npm-package-arg
```

```ts
import { createPackageInstaller, createPackageJournal } from '@bitakit/packages/server';

const installer = createPackageInstaller({
  directory: '/var/lib/my-app/runtime-packages',
  shared: { react: '19.3.0', '@bitakit/core': '0.2.7', '@bitakit/ui': '0.2.8' },
});
const artifact = await installer.install('trusted-package@1.2.3');
const journal = createPackageJournal('/var/lib/my-app/installations.sqlite', 'session-1');
```

The versions above illustrate exact host versions; use the versions your application actually
runs. Upgrade Core, Discovery and Packages together for the new APIs. The server entry requires
Node 24 or newer. `registry` optionally selects a standard npm registry. npm configuration owns
credentials. The host authorizes sources before calling `install`; there is no public install
HTTP endpoint supplied by this package.

npm resolves registry, Git and local package specs and installs their dependency graph with
lifecycle scripts disabled. A normal built package resolves its existing `bitakit.plugin` export
and manifest/sidecar ID. For source factories, `install(spec, { entry: './src/plugin.tsx',
pluginIds: ['notes'] })` explicitly selects a source entry; its default export is an ordinary
zero-argument plugin factory, optionally returning several plugins. This does not execute
arbitrary package build scripts or native toolchains. Multi-plugin packages must declare the
complete ID set; explicit IDs cannot contradict an existing single-plugin binding.

esbuild bundles ordinary dependencies and CSS/assets; Rollup emits a standard SystemJS module.
React, React DOM, Core and UI always stay external and require host bindings when imported. Other host packages in `shared` stay external. Their peer ranges are checked against the host and the
browser checks the prepared exact versions again. Statically resolvable imports are supported;
remote imports computed at runtime and native dependencies are outside this artifact format.
CSS assets use data URLs, covered by the stylesheet integrity digest. Packages still own their
CSS scoping; the loader does not sandbox global selectors.

`artifact.id` addresses immutable bytes under `installer.directory/<id>`. `installer.read(id)`
checks the descriptor digest and every file's integrity and works offline. Serve only declared
artifact files through the host's existing authenticated transport. Acquisition selectors,
resolved commit/integrity, npm lock and toolchain evidence stay in the private `evidence/`
directory; do not expose it as public content. Artifacts are retained until the operator removes
them; no automatic GC can delete the previous version or an interrupted recovery's bytes.

## Browser activation and recovery

Load [SystemJS](https://github.com/systemjs/systemjs) through your host's usual asset/CSP setup.
`createBrowserPackageProvider` from `@bitakit/packages/browser` accepts its standard loader,
actual host module namespaces and exact versions. For example, bind `react`,
`react/jsx-runtime`, `@bitakit/core` and `@bitakit/ui`; provide every additional shared subpath
listed by `artifact.imports`. Its `resolve(selection, signal)` callback returns an authorized
`{ artifact, baseURL }`, with a trailing slash on the immutable artifact directory URL.
SystemJS registry/import-map APIs share these actual instances. The adapter does not insert a
second React instance or a custom module bridge. JS and CSS use browser SRI; cross-origin
artifact responses need appropriate CORS, and CSP must permit their scripts/styles/data assets.

```ts
const packages = createPackageHost({
  runtime,
  dynamic: {
    provider, // createBrowserPackageProvider(...) or another trusted host artifact provider
    journal, // privileged journal through the host's authorized transport
    dataCompatibility: 'unchanged',
    health: async (pluginIds) => {
      /* await the host's actual UI/application readiness */
    },
  },
});
await packages.recover();
const result = await packages.reconcile({
  scope: 'session-1',
  packages: [{ name: artifact.name, version: artifact.version, artifact: artifact.id }],
});
```

Choose a catalog or dynamic mode for one host, and one coordinator/application session for one
journal key. A SQLite compare-and-swap rejects competing coordinators; this is not distributed
multi-browser deployment coordination. Call `recover()` on a fresh runtime before changing a
persisted installation. Recovering an interrupted forward update selects its recorded
predecessor; a committed update restores its new active artifact. Failed recovery keeps the
intent for intervention/retry. Neither scope strings nor artifact possession grant permission.

Dynamic mode checks all static IDs before importing code and uses Core's replacement preview
before stopping the old cohort. It stages CSS without enabling it, writes durable intent, then
awaits Core replacement and the optional host health check. On failure it restores the previous
cohort and checks its health too. `failed` with a restoration reason is still a failed requested
update; inspect `get()` and the journal. Failed cleanup or recovery blocks reuse. Providers and
foundational services retain Core's `restart-required` restrictions. External dependents are
refused; update their whole managed cohort together. A changed source requires explicit removal
before installation from the new source.

`dataCompatibility: 'unchanged'` is the storage owner's assertion that this operation needs no
data migration rollback. Code recovery recreates affected services; it does not snapshot their
in-memory state, undo module evaluation, reverse external effects or restore an application's
database. Unrelated instances and UI remain mounted. UI render readiness needs the host `health`
check; Core startup alone cannot prove a browser component rendered successfully. No automatic
update loop or stabilization timeout is assumed. Do not await management from `health`, plugin
hooks, affected Actions or disposers. `journal.close()` belongs to the privileged host shutdown.

For session shutdown, await `packages.dispose()` from host code. It releases managed plugins
and browser resources while preserving the journal's active selection for the next session.
It is also supported after a successful awaited `runtime.stop()`. Failed cleanup blocks reuse;
create a fresh host only after recovering those resources. To uninstall a selection, use
`reconcile({ scope, packages: [] })` instead: that intentionally persists an empty selection.
